questions.question: 1. The execution of a loop typically starts with:

explanations.a: Correct. Initialization statements set up the loop variables before the loop starts.
explanations.b: Incorrect. The loop body runs only after the setup and condition checks are complete.
explanations.c: Incorrect. The test condition is evaluated after the loop has been initialized.
explanations.d: Incorrect. The update step happens after the loop body during each pass.

questions.question: 2. The break statement is used to exit from:

explanations.a: Incorrect. This statement is meant for loop or switch control, not an if block.
explanations.b: Correct. The break statement is used to exit from a loop such as a for loop.
explanations.c: Incorrect. It exits the current loop or switch case, not the whole program.
explanations.d: Incorrect. It does not terminate the function directly.

questions.question: 3. A do-while loop is useful when we want the statements within the loop to be executed:

explanations.a: Incorrect. The loop body is evaluated before the condition is tested, so a single execution is not the defining feature.
explanations.b: Correct. A do-while loop always executes its body at least once before checking the condition.
explanations.c: Incorrect. The condition check happens after the body has already run once.
explanations.d: Incorrect. One of the listed choices matches the guaranteed execution behavior of a do-while loop.

questions.question: 4. In what sequence are initialization, testing, and execution of the body done in a do-while loop?

explanations.a: Correct. In a do-while loop, initialization happens first, then the body is executed, and then the condition is tested.
explanations.b: Incorrect. The setup step must occur before the loop body can start.
explanations.c: Incorrect. The condition is checked after the body in a do-while loop.
explanations.d: Incorrect. The loop has a standard sequence, and one of the listed options matches it.

questions.question: 5. Which of the following is not an infinite loop?

explanations.a: Incorrect. This loop does not move toward a terminating condition.
explanations.b: Incorrect. The controlling condition remains active across iterations.
explanations.c: Correct. This code is not an infinite loop because the loop variable is updated so that the condition eventually becomes false.
explanations.d: Incorrect. This option continues repeating without a valid termination condition.

questions.question: 6. Which of the following statements is used to take control to the beginning of the loop?

explanations.a: Incorrect. This is not a standard C loop-control keyword.
explanations.b: Incorrect. This keyword leaves the loop entirely rather than repeating the next iteration.
explanations.c: Correct. 'Continue' skips the rest of the loop body and starts the next iteration.
explanations.d: Incorrect. A standard loop-control keyword exists for this purpose.

questions.question: 7. How many '*' will this code print?

explanations.a: Incorrect. The loop control variable advances across repeated passes.
explanations.b: Incorrect. The loop executes more than one iteration for the given range.
explanations.c: Correct. The loop runs for i=1 and i=2, printing '*' twice.
explanations.d: Incorrect. The loop does not continue into a third pass.

questions.question: 8. Multiple initialization is not possible in a for loop.

explanations.a: Incorrect. The loop header allows multiple comma-separated expressions in its initialization section.
explanations.b: Correct. You can initialize multiple variables in a for loop, separated by commas.

questions.question: 9. A for loop can be converted into an equivalent while loop.

explanations.a: Correct. Any for loop can be rewritten as a while loop with equivalent logic.
explanations.b: Incorrect. Equivalent loop logic can be expressed using the while structure as well.

explanations.a: Incorrect. Nested iteration is a valid and common pattern in C.
